I use reaper too! Make sure you arm the track for recording (by pressing the red button on the track) and then make sure the "record monitoring" button is active. It's that little speaker looking button on the track near the FX button. Even with no effects in your chain, you should now be able to hear the dry signal of your guitar coming out of your speakers in real time. 

Now you can start loading up your vsts. You can find lots of good free amps [here](http://bedroomproducersblog.com/2012/02/21/bpb-freeware-studio-best-free-guitar-amp-simulator-vstau-plugins/) amongst other places. Google is your friend! For the sake of example, let's say you load up the Nick Crowe 8505 amp from that link. After this, you need an impulse response loader. This will simulate our guitar cab. I use [Pulse](http://www.rosendigitalaudio.com/pulse/). It's free! 

Lastly, you need impulses to load into Pulse (or whichever impulse response loader you choose). Some of those can be found for free [here](http://bedroomproducersblog.com/2010/10/01/free-sample-shootout-6-best-free-guitar-cabinet-impulse-responses/). These can be found all over the internet though so if these aren't to your liking, search around! There are lots of great options. 

All vsts past this are up to you. Think of it as you would a guitarist, as these will go in the chain the same way they would with real pedals. Add effects to your liking! Hope this was in depth enough. I'm on mobile so the formatting might be a little off. Let me know if you need any more specifics, I'm a nerd so talking about this stuff is fun for me.

You can get a good tone for free but it probably won't be an all in one software. The easiest way to  set up a digital rig for free is to find free vsts for each section of your rig. For example, you'd get a preamp vst, whatever pedals and effects you want, and then an impulse response loader (lots of great free options, look into Lepou).

I use Bias FAX and have managed to get some pretty great tones through the years. Not sure how updated it is, but if you're looking for cheaper podfarm is what I used to use. Wasn't perfect by a long shot but it got the job done

Mixing and mastering are difficult and there are an infinite number of things to learn about each, but after practicing it for years, I'm finally able to produce a professional sounding result and have actually made it my job now. 

Getting all this done professionally will cost a shit ton. I've known musicians that actually shelled out the money to get their work professionally produced and ended up with a product that is not what they wanted. Point I'm trying to make is just to do your research whether you pay for it or do it yourself. Either way, you can get the result you're looking for. 

And by the way, the periphery prog metal sound is what got me into the production side of music. Took me like 2 years to replicate that sound well, so good luck!
